newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols bounce as bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols bounce as bonds rally.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options inched up, bouncing from early lows, as the underlying bond market extended recent gains before pulling back slightly in late trade, dealers said.
"Vols are so low that it's hard to sell them down here," said a brokerage firm trader at the Chicago Board of Trade. "People are finally saying September vols under eight percent is unbelievable."
Implied volatility for September T-bond futures options was marginally higher on the day at about 8.0 percent shortly before the close.
Volatility for August options, which expire at the end of next week, was little changed at about 7.1 percent.

The bond market's rally since last week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which the Fed policy-makers kept interest rates steady, and benign June employment report has prompted short-covering in the upside strike prices, traders said.

In particular, shorts that had accumulated in August and September 114 calls were exposed to the painful negative gamma effect as September futures climbed to a high of 113-31/32 toward midsession before rowing back somewhat in late trade.
Shorter-dated, at-the-money options have the highest gamma, which gives quicker premium acceleration and bigger delta swings for delta-neutral volatility traders.

While some of the large-lot buying in the 114 calls appeared to be fresh volatility positions, some others done in spreads against 116 call selling appeared to be due to rolling up of short positions to higher strikes.
"There was a lot of buying in 114 calls, and they were selling 116 calls against some of those," a second CBOT trader said. "Different houses were doing it. I think they were covering shorts."

One firm was said to have bought 2,000 contracts of August 114 calls and sold 3,000 116 calls, while a few others were seen trading the same strike prices in 500 to 1,000 lots in a one-by-two ratio spread.
Traders said September futures still had a long way to go before reaching 116 but that the trend was clearly up.
"It seemed like earlier today people were looking to buy dips but there weren't any," the first CBOT trader said, adding that the late pullback was likely to have been caused by profit-taking.
In Eurodollar options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, volatilities were little changed as futures in the front months worked marginally firmer.
Implied volatility for December Eurodollar futures options was little changed at around 9.4 percent.
December futures rose 0.015 point to 94.060. Futures for June 1998 and beyond gained more, about 0.04 point each, but options activity in those months had yet to pick up, a CME trader said.
